text: At the mouth of Tessaly Fjord, where black water meets the granite shelves of Northfold’s western coast, the province’s newest energy landmark has quietly entered service. The Tessaly Fjord tidal plant, a lattice of sluice gates and submerged turbines engineered by Marrow Vale Hydro, is rated at 240 megawatts, enough, officials say, to supply roughly 180,000 homes through the winter peak. The project, first discussed in council papers in 2011 and delayed by storms, seabed surveys and a bruising permit fight, was completed after six years of construction. For longtime residents, the turning of the tide now carries a different meaning: not only the old rhythm of the fjord, but a measure of what the coast can yield.
